source.title: Kernel regression in high dimensions: Refined analysis beyond double descent
source.authors: Fanghui Liu; Zhenyu Liao; J. Suykens

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes and experimentally evaluates sample-size risk curves for kernel ridge regression, and argues that their shape can be double-descent-like, bell-shaped, or monotone depending on regularization and data eigenvalue decay.
record.gate_note: The study varies sample size n and reports theoretical and experimental risk or variance trends for kernel regression. Eigenvalue-decay plots and comparisons of kernel matrices with their linearizations do not report the claimed test-error trend and are not rows. Results cited from other papers are excluded. No deep-network size sweep or epoch sweep is reported.
record.test_reason: The study derives bias-variance bounds for high-dimensional kernel ridge regression as sample size n varies, and runs synthetic and real-data experiments. It argues the n-wise risk curve can be double-descent-like, bell-shaped or monotone depending on regularization and data eigen-decay. This bears directly on sample-wise non-monotonicity (V3) and on the regularization and variance dependence of the peak (V6). It does not vary model size, epochs or noise level.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, with one addition. The authors conclude that in high-dimensional KRR the bias bound decreases monotonically in n, while the variance bound is unimodal or decreasing depending on regularization and eigen-profile. The risk can therefore be double-descent-like, bell-shaped or monotone in n. They add that the second-descent minimum is lower than the first, and that MNIST shows monotone risk, possibly due to implicit kernel regularization.
record.recipe_differences: High-dimensional kernel ridge regression analysis using kernel linearization, bias-variance bounds, and synthetic and real-data experiments; it does not reproduce deep-network size or epoch sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk and variance trends depend on regularization level and data eigenvalue decay; the variance peak shifts with regularization in the harmonic-decay experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Theory: for fixed d, risk tends to zero as n→∞. In the double-descent case the n>d minimum is lower than the n<d minimum. The bias is nearly independent of d and the kernel type.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In high-dimensional KRR the second-descent risk minimum along n is below the first, and the shape of the risk curve is governed by the data spectrum rather than the kernel.

record.problems: The empirical curve descriptions are primarily qualitative and plotted values are not stated in the text. Synthetic results are reported across 10 trials without stated error bars or other uncertainty estimates. The authors note a mismatch between real-world data and technical Assumption 3. The study does not locate all risk peaks relative to the interpolation threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No other sample-size risk outcomes meeting the row criteria were left out. Eigenvalue-decay equivalence figures and kernel-versus-linearization comparisons do not report a test-error trend and were omitted.

untested.parts: Deep networks. Exact location of the peak relative to the interpolation threshold is not reported for the experiments.
Capacity sweeps past interpolation; only sample size n is varied.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Effect of label-noise level (σ fixed), multiple or triple peaks, and peak removal under optimally tuned regularization.

missing.what: Risk-curve shape (not just variance) under exponential eigen-decay. It is plotted in Figure 10 but its risk trend is not recorded.
Theoretical condition table: variance trend (increase, flat, decrease) as a function of ϑ, c̄, r*, n* and d for three eigen-decays. This shows where the peak sits relative to rank and d.

record.verdict_notes: The theoretical rows (r1–r3) rest on upper bounds and schematic figures, not measured risks. The authors show the V1 bound tracks the true variance in synthetic runs. All experimental results are qualitative curve descriptions, with no numbers or error bars in the text. The V6 limits_scope label in the record listed untested parts (noise, multiple peaks, optimal tuning); these are moved to untested.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model size and test error around the training-set interpolation threshold.
The study varies sample size for KRR, but does not establish that every reported peak is located near the interpolation threshold.
Capacity growth past the interpolation point; the study varies sample size rather than model capacity across model classes.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epochs, and sample size.
Noise levels are not varied; multiple or split peaks are not tested; the study does not establish disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
Recounting complexity by effective parameters to turn the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: kernel ridge regression (KRR) estimator
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes expected excess risk as sample size n changes under small or zero regularization.

conditions.value: conditions where the variance increases up to the rank/interpolation region and later falls
bias dominates at small n and decays fast

rows.value: The study says a double-descent curve can occur: risk falls, rises, and falls again.
rows.note: A conditional theoretical configuration, not a reported numeric estimate. The paper describes the peak as dependent on regularization and eigenvalue profile.
rows.check: Theoretical configuration built from upper bounds and illustrated by the schematic Figure 1(b); no measured curve. Requires small regularization and fast-decaying bias.

rows.subject: kernel ridge regression (KRR) estimator
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes expected excess risk and its variance as sample size n changes under different regularization levels.

conditions.value: small regularization for unimodal variance; level varies by setting

rows.measure: Expected excess risk curve and variance trend
rows.value: The risk can be bell-shaped; variance can increase and then decrease.
rows.note: The authors distinguish bell-shaped behavior from double descent; the variance trend depends on regularization and eigenvalue decay.
rows.check: Theoretical, bound-based. For V6 it supports the variance-driven peak: bell shape arises 'if the variance dominates'. Figure 1(c) is a schematic.

rows.subject: kernel ridge regression (KRR) estimator
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes expected excess risk as sample size n changes under large regularization.

conditions.value: large; n* is at most a constant c

rows.value: The risk can decrease monotonically with n; the variance can also decrease monotonically under large regularization.
rows.note: The decreasing risk is an explicit alternative to a rise-and-fall sample-size curve in these conditions.
rows.check: State should be absent, not reversed: a monotonically decreasing risk means no data-hurts rise, not the opposite effect. For V6 this is the predicted outcome, since large regularization removes the variance peak (n* ≤ c). Theoretical, from bounds and schematic Figure 1(d).

rows.subject: linearization of the polynomial kernel
rows.operation_detail: Varies sample size n and evaluates expected excess risk, bias, and variance.
rows.value: Bell-shaped; the variance dominates and the risk first increases and then decreases.
rows.note: The text describes the plotted trend but gives no numeric curve values. Results are validated across 10 trials.
rows.check: Linearized polynomial kernel with γ=0, d=500, harmonic decay. Risk measured as plotted MSE, with no numbers in the text.

rows.subject: linearization of the Gaussian kernel
rows.operation_detail: Varies sample size n and evaluates expected excess risk, bias, and variance.
rows.value: Bell-shaped; the variance dominates and the risk first increases and then decreases.
rows.note: The text describes the plotted trend but gives no numeric curve values. Results are validated across 10 trials.
rows.check: Same as r4, for the Gaussian kernel linearization.

rows.subject: linearization of the polynomial kernel
rows.operation_detail: Varies sample size n and evaluates expected excess risk, bias, and variance.
rows.value: Bell-shaped; as ϑ decreases, the variance peak occurs at smaller n.
rows.note: The text reports the peak shift for decreasing ϑ across the plotted settings; no numeric peak location is stated.
rows.check: At larger regularization (ϑ=1/3) the peak persists but moves to smaller n. For V6 this means regularization shifts the peak rather than removing it, so it is a scope qualification. The peak is no longer at the rank/threshold.

rows.subject: linearization of the Gaussian kernel
rows.operation_detail: Varies sample size n and evaluates expected excess risk, bias, and variance.
rows.value: Bell-shaped; as ϑ decreases, the variance peak occurs at smaller n.
rows.note: The text reports the peak shift for decreasing ϑ across the plotted settings; no numeric peak location is stated.
rows.check: Same as r6, for the Gaussian kernel linearization.

rows.subject: linearization of the polynomial kernel
rows.operation_detail: Varies sample size n and evaluates the expected excess risk and variance under polynomial eigenvalue decay.
rows.measure: Expected excess risk curve and variance trend
rows.value: The variance trend is unimodal and the risk curve is bell-shaped.
rows.note: The text reports the qualitative result across the shown settings, without numeric curve values.
rows.check: Polynomial-decay synthetic data (Appendix G.2, Fig. 9). The text reports unimodal V1 and a bell-shaped risk; trial count not stated.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix G.2; Figure 9 and discussion following Figure 10.

rows.subject: linearization of the polynomial kernel
rows.operation_detail: Varies sample size n and evaluates the variance bound and variance trend under exponential eigenvalue decay.

conditions.value: γ = 0; c̄ = 10⁻⁵ or 10⁻⁸ in the stated small-regularization examples

rows.value: The variance decreases monotonically with n, including in the stated small-regularization examples.
rows.note: This is a variance result, not by itself a reported test-error curve; it is included for V6's variance and regularization dependence.
rows.check: State should be absent, not reversed: under exponential decay the variance (bound V1) shows no peak, even at c̄=1e-5 or 1e-8. The paper reports no risk-curve shape here, so this row cannot inform V3. It shows the peak's existence depends on the data eigen-profile, not only on regularization.

rows.subject: kernel interpolation estimator
rows.operation_detail: Evaluates test performance as the number of data samples n changes.
rows.measure: Relative mean squared error on test data
rows.value: The risk curve is described as bell-shaped.
rows.note: The figure is described as an average over 10 trials; no numeric values or uncertainty estimates are stated.
rows.check: Kernel ridgeless regression (λ=0, implicit γ≠0) on a 1,000-example YearPredictionMSD subset, d=90. No explicit regularization is varied, so the V6 link is removed. Peak location relative to n=d is not stated.

rows.subject: kernel interpolation estimator
rows.operation_detail: Evaluates test performance as the number of data samples n changes.
rows.measure: Test performance; the text describes the risk curve as monotonically decreasing with n
rows.value: The risk curve is described as monotonically decreasing with n.
rows.note: The plotted metric is classification accuracy, while the text calls the curve a risk curve; no numeric values are given.
rows.check: State should be absent, not reversed: there is no rise, only a monotone improvement. The plotted metric is classification accuracy, although the text calls it a risk curve. The authors tentatively attribute the lack of a peak to implicit regularization γ (order 1e-3).

relationships.condition: KRR with small or moderate regularization and variance-dominated risk: synthetic harmonic and polynomial decay, and YearPredictionMSD
relationships.reason: Risk rises then falls with n, so more samples raise test error over part of the range (theory r1, r2; experiments r4, r5, r8, r10).
relationships.display_finding: Theory and experiments showed risk rising and then falling with sample count when variance dominated.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: KRR with small or moderate regularization and variance-dominated risk: synthetic harmonic and polynomial decay, and YearPredictionMSD
source_check.reason: r1–r2 describe conditional harmful-data regions; r4–r5, r8 and r10 report bell-shaped risk. The near-threshold interpretation is conditional on the peak location, rather than established for every experimental curve.

relationships.reason: Larger λ moves the peak left of the rank/threshold (r6, r7). Large regularization (theory, r3) and MNIST (r11) give monotone decrease with no data-hurts region.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing λ shifts the peak below the rank threshold, while sufficiently strong regularization and MNIST 3-vs-7 yield monotonically decreasing error.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: r3 and r11 describe monotone improvement; r6–r7 report a persistent peak shifted toward smaller sample sizes. The theoretical discussion allows the peak below the rank threshold.

relationships.condition: Harmonic- and polynomial-decay KRR with varying explicit regularization
relationships.reason: The peak comes from the variance term (r2, r4, r5, r8), and large regularization removes it, giving monotone risk (r3).
relationships.display_finding: The peak arose from variance, and sufficiently large regularization removed it, producing monotone risk.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Harmonic- and polynomial-decay KRR with varying explicit regularization
source_check.reason: r2, r4–r5 and r8 associate bell-shaped risk with dominant variance; r3 describes disappearance under large regularization. This supports those components of V6, without testing optimal tuning or multiple peaks.

relationships.reason: Moderate λ shifts the peak to smaller n rather than removing it (r6, r7). Under exponential decay no variance peak appears even with tiny λ (r9), so the peak depends on the data spectrum, not only on noise or regularization.
relationships.display_finding: Moderate λ shifted the peak toward smaller sample sizes, while exponential eigenvalue decay produced no variance peak even with tiny λ.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: r6–r7 do not test optimally tuned regularization, so a persistent peak at moderate regularization does not qualify that clause. r9 establishes monotone V1 under exponential decay, but V6 does not predict a peak for every spectrum. These facts do not establish the stated scope limitation.

relation.reason: Its own theoretical analysis and experiments examine sample-size risk curves, variance, and regularization.

tranche.reason: The study explicitly qualifies double-descent behavior through alternative risk shapes and dependence on regularization and eigenvalue decay.

source_check.notes: r1–r3 are conditional configurations inferred from bounds, not measured risk curves; r9 concerns the variance-bound term V1. MNIST plots accuracy, although the authors describe decreasing risk; optimal regularization and multiple peaks remain untested.

reader_labels.reason: Reported risk curves rise and then fall, so increasing n can worsen risk over part of the tested range (r4-r8, r10). The paper does not show that each peak is near the interpolation threshold.

reader_labels.reason: The authors also describe a monotonically decreasing risk curve under large regularization and for the MNIST setting, so the rise is not universal across conditions (r3, r11).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The analysis and experiments report unimodal variance under some settings and monotonically decreasing variance under others, with regularization changing peak location and sometimes removing the rise (r2-r9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The study does not vary noise, test multiple or split peaks, or demonstrate that an optimally tuned regularizer removes the peak; its evidence supports only a qualified regularization/variance dependence (r2-r9).
